title: The woman at the well (John 4:1–30)
hookLine: at noon, alone, a Samaritan woman has a long conversation with Jesus across an old divide

cards: A stranger on a train. A seatmate at a wedding. Sometimes the real talk is with someone nobody planned to meet.
This one happens at a well in Samaria, about the sixth hour, John says: noon, the heat at its worst. Jesus, tired from walking, sits on the edge of the well while his disciples go into town for food.
A woman comes out with a jar to draw water. Alone. And he speaks to her.

teach.b: He says, in the King James Bible: "Give me to drink." She's startled: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans."
Jews and Samaritans shared ancestors and the books of Moses, but had long been divided over where to worship God: Jerusalem, or Mount Gerizim, right above this well.
A Jewish teacher didn't usually ask a Samaritan woman for a drink.
He answers: "If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." Here's the wordplay.
Living water, in Greek and in everyday speech then, meant running water, fresh from a spring, not still water in a cistern. She hears the plain meaning: you don't even have a bucket.
He means water that becomes "a well of water springing up into everlasting life." Then he tells her about her own life: five husbands, and now a man who isn't her husband.
Some preachers have assumed she was a scandal, and that's why she came at noon. The text never says why. A woman then could be widowed, or sent away by a husband; John doesn't say what happened.

teach.h: A WELL OF WATER SPRINGING UP.
teach.b: What John does record is about twenty verses of question and answer, and it's with her. She goes back to town, leaving her jar behind: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?"
Orthodox Christians remember her as Photini, the enlightened one.

how: Many churches read the woman at the well during Lent, and Orthodox Christians keep a Sunday of the Samaritan Woman in the Easter season, honoring her as Saint Photini. Christians often read the story when speaking of baptism and of welcoming people across divides.

games.q: you're the woman at the well. a stranger has just told you things about your life no stranger could know. what do you do?
o: leave your jar and run to tell the whole town.
finish drawing water and go home quietly.
games.why: she leaves her waterpot and goes into the city: come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did.

practice: Think of one person you mostly talk to in passing, a parent, a coworker, a neighbor, someone who serves you coffee, and picture sitting down with them, no clock, no phone.
What might you ask that you never have, and what might they tell you? If you pray, you can ask for patience to listen.

wordCard.voice: Samaritan. The woman Jesus meets at the well, from a people long divided from the Jews, whom he still asks, in the heat of noon, for a drink.

orig.note: Greek: living water. In everyday speech, running water from a spring; in John, a gift that springs up inside.

carryVoice: Your line: living water. Tomorrow, a hillside, a hungry crowd and a boy's lunch. Day fifty-three, done.
